To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) for bimatrix games, we can identify an approximate Nash equilibrium while querying just a constant fraction of pure-strategies (and their associated payoffs), and 2) for congestion games with parallel links, we can identify a pure Nash equilibrium by querying only a constant fraction of the cost functions.
for congestion games, a small number of strategy profiles and payoff values are sufficient for learning the cost functions and an equilibrium.

(1) for bimatrix games and graphical games, the query complexity is exponential in the number of players; (2) for congestion games on DAGs, the query complexity for learning the cost functions and for identifying an equilibrium are polynomial in the number of links; (3) for parallel links, the query complexity to learn an equilibrium is polynomial in the number n of players.
In summary, our research is concerned with
learning the structure of a game (the cost functions), rather than learning the payoffs.
the computational complexity of learning equibilia of games.
the computational and algorithmic aspects of empirical game theory, and the connections between the two.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
for symmetric games with a small number of players, the query complexity is small.
, in contrast to the experimental setting, the learning complexity of equilibria in congestion games is not necessarily high.
the learning complexity of equilibria of symmetric congestion games is much lower than their computational complexity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that the empirical analysis problem for congestion games is much easier than the classical game-theoretical analysis problem.
the query complexity of computing equilibria is polynomial in the number of players and links, and logarithmic in the number of strategy profiles.
we can learn an equilibrium of a congestion game on an arbitrary network with n nodes and m links in time polynomial in m, n and the number of queries, even if the cost functions are unknown.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the query complexity for the computational learning model is significantly lower than that of the on-line model, and that it is not necessary to have access to the entire game in order to compute an equilibrium.
learning the equilibrium of games is often possible with a small number of payoff queries, which may be significantly smaller than the number of pure-strategy profile queries.
the learning model can be a useful framework for studying empirical game-theoretical learning, and may lead to better algorithms for the empirical setting.
